# Slack vs Element (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Element are two popular communication platforms designed for teams and organizations. This comparison is beneficial for teams considering switching from Slack to Element, particularly those valuing data ownership and seeking a self-hosted solution. The core use case for both tools is team collaboration, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Element is free and self-hosted, while Slack charges per user.
* Data ownership: Element allows teams to own their data, while Slack stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Element requires more technical expertise to set up, while Slack is easier to get started with.
* Scalability: Slack is more scalable, with better support for large teams, while Element can be more challenging to scale.
* Integration with GitHub: Slack has native integration with GitHub, while Element requires a third-party bridge.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Element |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1450-$3000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Slack
* Easy to set up and use
* Native integration with many third-party apps
* Scalable and reliable
* Good customer support
* Limited control over data
### Element
* Free and self-hosted
* Teams own their data
* Highly customizable
* Secure and private
* Requires technical expertise to set up

## When to Choose Each
Slack is a good choice for large teams that need a scalable and reliable communication platform, and are willing to pay for it. It's also a good option for teams that don't require a high level of control over their data. Element, on the other hand, is a good choice for teams that value data ownership and want a self-hosted solution. It's also a good option for teams with technical expertise and a desire for a high level of customization.
Element is suitable for small to medium-sized teams that want a free and self-hosted solution. It's also a good option for teams that require a high level of security and privacy. However, it may not be the best choice for teams that require a high level of scalability and reliability.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack API or a third-party tool.
2. Set up an Element server and configure it to your needs.
3. Import your Slack data into Element using the Element import tool.
4. Configure any necessary bridges or integrations.
5. Test your Element setup to ensure everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
Element is not yet production-ready for most users, as it still lacks some of the features and polish of Slack. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Element's scalability can be a challenge, particularly for large teams. However, for teams that value data ownership and are willing to put in the effort to set up and configure Element, it can be a good choice.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that don't need advanced features
* Teams that value data ownership and want a self-hosted solution
* Technical teams that can handle the setup and configuration of Element
* Teams that don't require native integration with GitHub
* Teams with limited budgets that want a free communication platform

## FAQ
### Can I use Element for free?
Yes, Element is free and self-hosted. You can download and install it on your own server.
### Is Element as scalable as Slack?
No, Element can be more challenging to scale, particularly for large teams.
### Can I integrate Element with GitHub?
Yes, but it requires a third-party bridge.
### Is Element secure and private?
Yes, Element is designed with security and privacy in mind, and teams have full control over their data.
### Can I migrate my Slack data to Element?
Yes, you can export your Slack data and import it into Element using the Element import tool.

# Slack vs Mattermost (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Mattermost are two popular communication platforms designed for teams and organizations. This comparison is beneficial for teams looking to switch from Slack to Mattermost, particularly those prioritizing data ownership and self-hosting capabilities. The core use case for both tools is team collaboration, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Mattermost offers a free, self-hosted option, while Slack charges per user.
* Data ownership: Mattermost allows teams to host their data on their own servers, while Slack stores data on its proprietary servers.
* Setup complexity: Slack is generally easier to set up, with a more streamlined onboarding process, while Mattermost requires more technical expertise for self-hosting.
* Scalability: Both platforms can scale to support large teams, but Mattermost's self-hosted option provides more flexibility for customization and scaling.
* Integration: Slack has a more extensive library of integrations with third-party apps, while Mattermost has a more limited selection, although it is growing.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Mattermost |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT / AGPL |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,450-$3,000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Slack
* Easy to set up and use
* Extensive library of integrations with third-party apps
* Strong support for mobile devices
* Robust search functionality
* Limited control over data storage and security
### Mattermost
* Free, self-hosted option
* High degree of customization and control over data
* Strong support for developer communities
* Growing library of integrations with third-party apps
* Steeper learning curve due to self-hosting requirements

## When to Choose Each
### Slack
Slack is a good choice for teams that prioritize ease of use and a wide range of integrations with third-party apps. It is well-suited for small to medium-sized teams that do not require a high degree of customization or control over their data. Slack is also a good option for teams that are already familiar with its interface and do not want to invest time in setting up a self-hosted solution.
### Mattermost
Mattermost is a good choice for teams that prioritize data ownership and control, as well as customization and scalability. It is well-suited for larger teams or organizations that require a high degree of flexibility and customization. Mattermost is also a good option for developer communities or teams that require strong support for coding and development workflows.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack API or a third-party tool.
2. Set up a Mattermost server and configure it to your needs.
3. Import your Slack data into Mattermost using the Mattermost API or a third-party tool.
4. Configure your Mattermost instance to match your Slack setup, including channels, users, and integrations.
5. Test your Mattermost instance to ensure that all features and integrations are working as expected.

## Our Take
Mattermost is a production-ready alternative to Slack for many users, offering a high degree of customization and control over data. However, it is worth noting that Mattermost's self-hosting requirements can be a barrier for some teams, particularly those without extensive technical expertise. For teams that prioritize ease of use and a wide range of integrations, Slack may still be the better choice.

One specific technical limitation worth knowing before switching to Mattermost is its limited support for certain types of file sharing and storage. While Mattermost offers robust support for code sharing and collaboration, it may not be the best choice for teams that require extensive file sharing and storage capabilities.

Overall, we recommend Mattermost for teams that prioritize data ownership and control, as well as customization and scalability. Teams that are already familiar with Slack and do not require a high degree of customization or control over their data may want to stick with Slack.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that require a free, self-hosted solution and do not need extensive integrations with third-party apps.
* Medium-sized teams (10-50 users) that prioritize data ownership and control, and are willing to invest time in setting up a self-hosted solution.
* Large teams (more than 50 users) that require a high degree of customization and scalability, and are willing to invest in technical expertise to support a self-hosted solution.
* Developer communities that require strong support for coding and development workflows.
* Teams that do not require extensive file sharing and storage capabilities.

## FAQ
### Can I use Mattermost for free?
Yes, Mattermost offers a free, self-hosted option that can be used by teams of any size.
### Is Mattermost as easy to use as Slack?
No, Mattermost has a steeper learning curve due to its self-hosting requirements and more extensive customization options.
### Can I integrate Mattermost with third-party apps?
Yes, Mattermost has a growing library of integrations with third-party apps, although it is not as extensive as Slack's.
### Can I export my Slack data and import it into Mattermost?
Yes, you can export your Slack data using the Slack API or a third-party tool, and import it into Mattermost using the Mattermost API or a third-party tool.
### Is Mattermost suitable for large teams?
Yes, Mattermost is suitable for large teams, offering a high degree of customization and scalability.

# Discord vs Element (2026)

## Overview
Discord and Element are communication platforms designed for community building and team collaboration. This comparison is beneficial for individuals and teams seeking a secure, feature-rich, and scalable communication solution. Those considering switching from Discord to Element are likely motivated by the desire for greater control over their data and a self-hosted solution.

## Key Differences
* **Cost**: Discord offers a free plan with optional upgrades, while Element is free and open-source, with costs limited to self-hosting.
* **Data Ownership**: Element provides full data ownership, as users host their own servers, whereas Discord stores data on its proprietary servers.
* **Setup Complexity**: Discord is generally easier to set up, with a more straightforward user interface, while Element requires more technical expertise for self-hosting.
* **Scalability**: Both platforms are scalable, but Element's self-hosted nature allows for more flexibility in terms of server configuration and customization.
* **Integration with Matrix**: Element has native integration with the Matrix protocol, allowing for seamless communication with other Matrix-compatible platforms, whereas Discord does not.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Discord | Element |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $9.99/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $4.99/month (billed annually) | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $4.99/month (billed annually) | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Discord
* Easy to set up and use
* Large user base and community
* Feature-rich, with screen sharing and video conferencing
* Mobile apps available
* Limited data ownership and control
### Element
* Self-hosted, with full data ownership and control
* Open-source and customizable
* Integrates with Matrix protocol
* Secure, with end-to-end encryption
* Steeper learning curve and more complex setup

## When to Choose Each
Discord is suitable for teams and communities that prioritize ease of use, a large user base, and a wide range of features, such as gaming communities or small businesses. Element, on the other hand, is ideal for organizations that require full data ownership, customizability, and security, such as large enterprises or government institutions.

Element is a better choice for teams that value self-hosting, data control, and integration with the Matrix protocol. This includes teams with high security requirements, such as financial institutions or healthcare organizations. Additionally, teams with existing infrastructure and technical expertise may prefer Element for its customizability and flexibility.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Discord server data using the Discord API or a third-party tool.
2. Set up an Element server, either self-hosted or through a hosting provider.
3. Import your Discord data into Element using the Element import tool or a compatible Matrix client.
4. Configure your Element server settings, including user roles, channels, and integrations.
5. Invite your users to join your new Element server and assist with the transition.

## Our Take
Element is not yet production-ready for most users, as it still lacks some of the polish and user-friendliness of Discord. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is Element's current lack of support for certain media formats, such as video conferencing. However, for teams that require self-hosting, data control, and security, Element is a clear choice, and we recommend switching from Discord to take advantage of these features.

## Who Should Switch
* Small to medium-sized businesses seeking self-hosting and data control
* Gaming communities that do not require Discord's proprietary features
* Teams with high security requirements, such as financial institutions
* Organizations with existing infrastructure and technical expertise
* Communities that do not need Discord's large user base or social features

## FAQ
### Can I use Element for free?
Yes, Element is free and open-source, with costs limited to self-hosting.
### Is Element compatible with Discord?
No, Element uses the Matrix protocol, which is not compatible with Discord's proprietary protocol.
### Can I migrate my Discord data to Element?
Yes, you can export your Discord data and import it into Element using compatible tools.
### Is Element suitable for large teams?
Yes, Element is scalable and suitable for large teams, with support for self-hosting and customizability.
### Does Element support video conferencing?
Not yet, Element currently lacks support for certain media formats, including video conferencing.

# Notion vs AppFlowy (2026)

## Overview
Notion and AppFlowy are two popular tools used for note-taking, project management, and team collaboration. This comparison is beneficial for individuals and teams looking to switch from Notion to AppFlowy, particularly those seeking a self-hosted solution with more control over their data. The core use case for both tools is to provide an all-in-one workspace for teams to manage their work, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more flexibility and data ownership.

* Cost: Notion charges $8-$20 per user per month, while AppFlowy is free.
* Data ownership: AppFlowy allows users to self-host their data, giving them full control and ownership, whereas Notion stores data on its proprietary servers.
* Setup complexity: Notion has a more user-friendly interface and is easier to set up, while AppFlowy requires more technical expertise to self-host.
* Scalability: AppFlowy is designed to be highly scalable, making it suitable for large teams and enterprises, whereas Notion's scalability is limited by its proprietary nature.
* Integration: Notion has a more extensive library of integrations with third-party apps, while AppFlowy has a more limited but growing list of integrations.

| Aspect | Notion | AppFlowy |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $8-$20/user/month | Free |
| License | Proprietary | GPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $400-$1000/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1600-$4000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Notion:**
* Easy to use and set up
* Extensive library of integrations
* User-friendly interface
* Limited control over data
* Proprietary license
**AppFlowy:**
* Self-hosting option for full data control
* Highly scalable
* Free and open-source
* Steeper learning curve
* Limited integrations with third-party apps

## When to Choose Each
Notion is suitable for small to medium-sized teams that prioritize ease of use and a wide range of integrations. It is ideal for teams that do not require self-hosting and are willing to compromise on data ownership. AppFlowy, on the other hand, is designed for larger teams and enterprises that require high scalability, self-hosting, and full control over their data. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that AppFlowy's search functionality is not as robust as Notion's. However, for teams that require self-hosting and full control over their data, AppFlowy is a viable alternative to Notion, and we recommend switching to AppFlowy if you have the technical expertise to handle the setup and maintenance.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams of 10 or fewer users who do not require extensive integrations
* Teams that prioritize data ownership and self-hosting
* Enterprises with 100 or more users who require high scalability
* Technical teams with expertise in self-hosting and maintenance
* Teams that do not require a wide range of integrations with third-party apps

## FAQ

title: Notion vs Obsidian
comparison_markdown:
# Notion vs Obsidian

## Overview

All-in-one workspace combining notes, databases, wikis, and project management. is a popular proprietary tool in the productivity space. Obsidian is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Notion costs $8-$20/user/month; Obsidian is Free (local use)
- **License**: Notion is Proprietary; Obsidian is Proprietary (free personal)
- **Data ownership**: Obsidian can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: Obsidian eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: Obsidian has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Notion | Obsidian |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | $8-$20/user/month | Free (local use) |
| License | Proprietary | Proprietary (free personal) |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | ~$400/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | ~$1,600/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Notion

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Obsidian

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Notion if:** Notion is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose Obsidian if:** Obsidian is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Export your data from Notion in its standard export format, review Obsidian import documentation, and plan a pilot period where both tools run in parallel.

## Our Take

Obsidian is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Notion tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Obsidian instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Notion, switching to self-hosted Obsidian will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Notion until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Notion paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Obsidian free to use?
Yes. Obsidian is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Notion to Obsidian?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Notion data, follow the Obsidian import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Obsidian get regular updates?
Yes. Obsidian has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Obsidian without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if Obsidian development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced June 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Notion](https://notion.so) and [Obsidian](https://obsidian.md) before making decisions.*

However, for teams that prioritize data control and customization, Logseq is a clear winner, and we recommend switching to Logseq if you're a technical team with more than 10 users.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams of 5-10 users who don't need Notion's calendar feature
* Medium-sized teams of 10-50 users who want more control over their data
* Large teams of 50+ users who require self-hosting and customization options
* Technical teams who prioritize data control and customization
* Organizations with strict data security and compliance requirements

## FAQ
### Can I self-host Logseq?
Yes, Logseq can be self-hosted, giving you full control over your data and customization options.

Yes, Logseq is completely free and open-source.

title: GitHub vs GitLab
comparison_markdown:
# GitHub vs GitLab

## Overview

GitHub is the world largest code hosting platform, owned by Microsoft, with 100 million developers. GitLab is a complete DevOps platform that can be fully self-hosted, offering everything from Git hosting to CI/CD and container registries.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: GitHub free tier is generous; GitLab Community Edition is fully free to self-host
- **CI/CD**: GitLab has more powerful built-in CI/CD pipelines; GitHub Actions is catching up
- **Self-hosting**: GitLab is designed to be self-hosted; GitHub Enterprise self-hosted is expensive
- **Feature scope**: GitLab is a complete DevSecOps platform; GitHub focuses on developer collaboration
- **Community**: GitHub has a dramatically larger open-source community and project discoverability

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | GitHub | GitLab |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $7-$21/user | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT (CE) |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### GitHub

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### GitLab

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [gitlabhq/gitlabhq](https://github.com/gitlabhq/gitlabhq) * ~24k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose GitHub if:** GitHub suits open-source projects wanting maximum community visibility or teams deeply integrated with GitHub Actions workflows.

**Choose GitLab if:** GitLab self-hosted is ideal for enterprises needing full control over their DevOps stack or regulated industries.

## Migration Path

GitLab provides a GitHub importer that migrates repositories, issues, PRs, wikis, and milestones. Update CI configuration from GitHub Actions to GitLab CI/CD YAML format.

## Our Take

GitLab is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid GitHub tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your GitLab instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for GitHub, switching to self-hosted GitLab will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on GitHub until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated GitHub paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is GitLab free to use?
Yes. GitLab is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from GitHub to GitLab?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your GitHub data, follow the GitLab import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does GitLab get regular updates?
Yes. GitLab has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use GitLab without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if GitLab development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced June 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [GitHub](https://github.com) and [GitLab](https://gitlab.com) before making decisions.*

title: GitHub vs Gitea

# GitHub vs Gitea (2026)

## Overview
GitHub and Gitea are two popular version control platforms used for software development. They offer a range of features that benefit developers, teams, and organizations. The core use case for both tools is to manage and track code changes, and the key reason someone would switch from GitHub to Gitea is to gain more control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: GitHub offers a free plan with limited features, while Gitea is free and open-source, allowing for self-hosting.
* Data Ownership: Gitea provides full control over data, whereas GitHub stores data on its servers.
* Setup Complexity: Gitea requires more technical expertise for setup, while GitHub offers a more user-friendly interface.
* Scalability: GitHub is more scalable, with built-in support for large teams and enterprises, while Gitea may require more configuration for large-scale deployments.
* Feature Difference: GitHub offers integrated project management tools, while Gitea relies on third-party integrations for similar functionality.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | GitHub | Gitea |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $7-$21/user | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $350-$1050/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1400-$4200/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**GitHub:**
* Easy to use and set up
* Integrated project management tools
* Large community and support resources
* Scalable for large teams and enterprises
* Limited control over data
**Gitea:**
* Free and open-source
* Self-hosting option for full data control
* Customizable and extensible
* Low costs for small to medium-sized teams
* Limited integrated project management tools

## When to Choose Each
GitHub is suitable for large teams and enterprises that require integrated project management tools and are willing to pay for the service. It is also a good choice for developers who prioritize ease of use and are already familiar with the platform. Gitea, on the other hand, is ideal for small to medium-sized teams, open-source projects, or organizations that require full control over their data and are comfortable with self-hosting.

## Migration Path
1. Export your GitHub repository using the GitHub Archive format.
2. Set up a Gitea instance on your own server or use a hosted service.
3. Use the Gitea import tool to migrate your repository from the GitHub Archive format.
4. Configure any necessary integrations or settings in Gitea.
5. Test your migrated repository to ensure everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
Gitea is a production-ready alternative to GitHub for many users, offering a high degree of customizability and control over data. However, one technical limitation worth noting is that Gitea's integrated project management tools are not as robust as those offered by GitHub. For teams that require advanced project management features, GitHub may still be the better choice. However, for small to medium-sized teams or organizations that prioritize data control and cost-effectiveness, Gitea is a clear winner.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that do not need integrated project management tools
* Open-source projects that require full control over their data
* Organizations with limited budgets that want to reduce costs
* Teams that are already familiar with self-hosting and server management
* Developers who prioritize customizability and extensibility

## FAQ
### Is Gitea free?
Yes, Gitea is free and open-source, allowing for self-hosting and customization.
### Can I migrate my GitHub repository to Gitea?
Yes, you can export your GitHub repository and import it into Gitea using the Gitea import tool.
### Does Gitea offer integrated project management tools?
No, Gitea relies on third-party integrations for project management functionality.
### Is Gitea suitable for large teams and enterprises?
Not yet, as Gitea may require more configuration for large-scale deployments and lacks some of the integrated features offered by GitHub.
### Can I use Gitea for private repositories?
Yes, Gitea allows for private repositories and offers full control over data access and permissions.
